title: Opinion: In Carney’s major projects push, is he overlooking Indigenous rights?
byline: Harold Calla; Mylon Ollila; Lawrence Schembri
html:
Harold Calla is executive chair of the First Nations Financial Management Board.

Mylon Ollila is director of strategic opportunities of the First Nations Financial Management Board.

Lawrence Schembri is a board member of the Tulo Centre of Indigenous Economics and a former deputy governor of the Bank of Canada.

This essay is part of the Prosperity’s Path series. In a time of geopolitical instability and a shifting world order, the challenges facing Canada's economy have only gotten more visible, numerous and intense. This series brings solutions.

Mark Carney’s government has championed the development of major projects as a matter of urgent national interest. The Canada Investment Summit showcased a whopping 167 of them, and a unique intensity infuses the Prime Minister’s rhetoric.

As the Carneyisms go, we have to “build, baby, build,” with an “ambition and speed not seen in generations,” so that we can “give ourselves more than anyone else can take away” and be “masters of our destiny.”

Indeed, major projects in natural-resource development, electricity generation and transmission, and transportation are critical to diversifying Canada’s trade and ensuring our future prosperity.

Canada must leverage its comparative advantage to enhance its economic resilience in an uncertain and rapidly changing world. Through the Building Canada Strong Act, the Carney government has reduced barriers to natural-resource development to get major projects built faster.

Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson at the AFN 2026 Annual General Assembly.Justin Tang/The Canadian Press

But these major projects are overwhelmingly located on or near traditional Indigenous territory. Although the act says that Indigenous rights will be respected and both Mr. Carney and Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson have stressed the importance of Indigenous partnerships, the act contains nothing new about how to achieve such partnerships. That is a problem for the projects.

Indigenous leaders have expressed concern that the Carney government is treating Indigenous rights as an issue to be managed after major projects have been selected and approved. They argue that these rights should be respected by consulting with the affected Indigenous communities from the get-go and by encouraging their participation. Otherwise, Canada risks introducing the delays and uncertainty it wants to avoid.

Indigenous rights are constitutionally recognized and protected. The Crown has a duty to consult whenever an action could adversely affect treaty and Indigenous rights and to accommodate where necessary. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act strengthened this duty through its requirement to “consult and cooperate” with the goal of “free, prior, and informed consent.”

Our research has found that First Nations located close to major projects are the most likely to have equity participation in major projects. That may sound obvious, but the takeaway is important for advancing those projects: It suggests that strength of property rights enhances bargaining power, supporting the case for obtaining Indigenous consent and shared project ownership.

Our resource industries have plenty of cautionary tales of court injunctions halting work and shaking investor confidence, such as mining company Solid Gold Resources Corp., which bypassed the duty to consult only to abandon its project when investor finance evaporated.

Putting off engagement, only to present Indigenous communities with final take-it-or-leave-it offers, risks costly disputes and delays after significant investments have already been made.

If the Carney government wants to build projects faster, it should consider how to effectively engage affected Indigenous communities. This would require a meaningful equity share and a fair return, not just symbolic ownership. For example, Ottawa’s proposal to offer Indigenous groups a 15-per-cent ownership stake in the Trans Mountain pipeline has received a lukewarm response from some Indigenous organizations, who argue that it falls short of meaningful participation.

In October, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the planned Pacific Link pipeline would be designated a project in the national interest. The decision was met with immediate opposition from Indigenous communities across Alberta and B.C.Greg Halinda/The Canadian Press

The path to greater project certainty cannot be attained by shortchanging Indigenous engagement, but through effective partnerships. When Indigenous communities participate in major projects as equity owners, they have direct interest in long-term project success. Indigenous equity participation leads to shared governance, continuing dialogue and decision-making, and it signals to investors that projects will proceed with reduced risk and lower cost. The research shows that Indigenous participation in major projects speeds up development, increases returns and improves environmental sustainability.

If equity partnerships are such an obvious solution, why don’t we see more of them?

The key barrier is not willingness on the part of Indigenous communities. It is access to finance. Our own research across a database of 129 major projects with Indigenous equity ownership finds that external support for Indigenous finance is associated with project success. While Indigenous financial institutions are making great strides, Indigenous governments face constraints that other borrowers do not. For First Nations, the Indian Act undermines property rights and the ability to borrow against land and other assets on reserve. As a result, many First Nations communities have far fewer financing options even when strong investment opportunities exist.

The challenge is significant. We estimate that Indigenous participation in the 167 Investment Summit projects would require $30-billion to $50-billion in equity financing. Canada’s existing Indigenous loan guarantee program, while an important step, is set at only $10-billion.

If Canada is serious about Indigenous equity partnerships, it should be equally serious about establishing the financial tools needed to support them.

That means either increasing Indigenous loan guarantees, which are conditional liabilities of the government, or, better still, creating Indigenous-led financing vehicles or institutions that could issue their own bonds to global capital markets to finance equity stakes in major projects.

Our research shows that grants and loan guarantees have been effective in supporting early-stage project participation and equity partnerships.

Alternatively, the First Nations Finance Authority is developing a process to lend to Indigenous-owned investment vehicles for major projects. Ottawa should support this initiative, and quickly.

National Indigenous organizations have also called for the creation of an Indigenous Development Finance Organization capable of mobilizing capital at the scale increasingly required by modern projects. Such an agency could also serve as an honest broker in major project deal-making between project proponents and First Nations governments. For example, the Alberta Indigenous Opportunities Corporation has facilitated Indigenous ownership in major projects by acting as a trusted intermediary. By seeking mutually beneficial outcomes, it has been able to get deals done quickly, regardless of the number of communities involved, and with significant Indigenous ownership.

Canada should build on these successes at a national scale because they reduce uncertainty and risk and generate sufficient returns for all parties: private-sector project proponents, Indigenous communities, and federal and provincial governments. These Indigenous financing initiatives are financially self-sustaining; they are not another government spending program.

The Carney government is right that major projects are critical to our future prosperity. To expedite their development, Indigenous communities should be engaged as early as possible and their meaningful participation empowered. The path to major project development, and prosperity for all Canadians, is through Indigenous partnerships.
summary: If Ottawa wants to build projects faster, it should consider how to effectively engage affected Indigenous communities
